events.title: Economists confirm a recession
events.description: Researchers identify December 2007 as the end of the expansion. The downturn had begun before your September 2008 decision.

events.title: The Fed lowers rates close to zero
events.description: The Federal Reserve sets its short-term target at 0–0.25% as the economy weakens and borrowing remains difficult.

events.title: Economists date the recession’s end
events.description: Researchers identify June 2009 as the low point. Recovery beginning does not mean conditions have already returned to normal.

events.title: Apple plans to resume dividends
events.description: The company announces payments to shareholders and plans to buy back shares. The first dividend follows in August.

events.title: The Fed continues buying financial assets
events.description: It keeps its short-term interest-rate target near zero and continues buying bonds to support the economy.

what_happened_next.text:
All three company investments ended above their September 2008 starting values. Apple gained about 331%, much more than Microsoft’s 42% or Exxon Mobil’s 25%. The result came after a frightening period: banks and other businesses were in trouble, the Federal Reserve cut interest rates close to zero, and the recession lasted into 2009.

The companies had different sources of business. Apple sold 31.2 million iPhones in its June 2013 quarter and reported $6.9 billion in net income. Microsoft’s revenue grew 10% in its June quarter as business software and server products helped offset a weaker PC market. ExxonMobil reported $44.9 billion in earnings for 2012, up 9% from 2011. The facts describe business performance; they do not prove that any single event caused the share returns.

A group that tracks the U.S. economy later dated the recession’s end to June 2009, but did not announce that until September 2010. By September 2013, interest rates were still very low. Getting a positive five-year result did not make the frightening months easy to ignore or recovery certain. The stocks went through years of change before the final comparison could be made.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: People read about a rejected plan to help banks, emergency help for AIG, and rising unemployment. They also followed the election, events in Pakistan, science, music, and new technology.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: The crisis brought sharp falls and long months of worry. Later, the economy began to recover, but the three companies did not grow in the same way. A five-year result can hide how much an investment changed on the way.
reflection.what_faded_away: The rescue-plan vote and campaign news soon moved on. The crisis did not end after one vote; more decisions and a long recovery followed. New products and music also gave way to later stories.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: In September 2008, no one knew how long the crisis would last, when interest rates would rise again, or how Apple, Microsoft, and Exxon Mobil would change. All three investments ended higher after five years, but that did not make the road there obvious.

hot:2008-09:apple.text: In July 2013, Apple reported $35.3 billion in sales and $6.9 billion in net profit for its June quarter. It sold 31.2 million iPhones, a record for a June quarter, but iPad sales were lower than a year earlier. Its phone business was growing even as some other devices slowed.

hot:2008-09:microsoft.text: Microsoft’s June-quarter sales rose 10% to $19.9 billion in 2013. Business software and server products helped offset a weak PC market. Its new Surface RT tablets also struggled: Microsoft recorded a $900 million charge to reduce the value of unsold stock.

hot:2008-09:exxonmobil.text: ExxonMobil reported $44.9 billion in profit for 2012, up 9% from 2011. It also spent a record $39.8 billion on equipment, projects and exploration. Strong earnings gave it money to develop new oil and gas supplies and return cash to shareholders.
